# FDG8062

> AVOID using `System.DBNull`. Prefer `Nullable<T>` instead.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 8.8 Nullable&lt;T>.

## How it is checked

- Check: judgment
- Automatic fix: no
- Severity: library warning, application warning, test warning
- Status: draft

Analyzer candidate rejected: DBNull.Value is what ADO.NET returns and takes for database nulls, so uses of it in data-access code are not a design choice, and the Castro annotation keeps DBNull when its null propagation semantics matter.

## From the book

> **Pablo Castro:** `Nullable<T>` is, in general, a better representation of optional database values. One thing to consider, though, is that while `Nullable<T>` gives you the ability to represent null values, you don’t get database null operational semantics. Specifically, you don’t get null propagation through operators and functions. If you deeply care about the propagation semantics, consider sticking with `DBNull`.
